summaries.summary: The paper addresses segmenting an unordered text document into sections by clustering sentences around identified keywords using keyword and cluster similarity.
TextRank algorithm BIBREF0 extracts keywords from a text document using graph-based global information, and a cluster is generated for every keyword.
Cluster generation uses cosine similarity of Google's USE (Universal Sentence Encoder) BIBREF1 embeddings, with better cluster quality when keyword and mapped-sentence similarities are combined.
The approach is tested by jumbling sentence order, processing the unordered document, and comparing output similarity with the original document.
Related work covers topic-based sentence retrieval, query-relevant graph approaches, incremental integrated graphs, master sequences, summary sequencing, and sentence ordering.
The paper aims to generate sections/clusters from an unordered document and claims this is the first formal attempt to address the problem.
The proposed model takes an unordered document, extracts keywords using TextRank algorithm BIBREF0 into list $K$, and uses them as cluster centroids.
The model maps the most relevant sentence to each keyword in $K$ using cosine similarity of Google's USE embeddings, then maps remaining sentences.
$S_1(x,y)$ measures current sentence $x$ similarity with keyword $y$, while $S_2(x,y)$ is maximum similarity with sentences already mapped to $y$.
Equation 1 defines $S(x,y)= t*S_1(x,y) + (1-t)*S_2(x,y)$.
Each sentence $x$ is mapped by $Max_y (S(x,y))$, keywords and sentences are clustered, and $t$ is empirically fixed to $0.25$.
The proposed $Sim1$ and $Sim2$ metrics compare original sections with output sections/clusters using maximum similarity and weighted means.
Experiments use five sets of 100 randomly chosen wiki documents, each randomly restructured as model input and compared against the original input document.
Table 1 compares $Sim1$ and $Sim2$ with baseline results using $t$ value as 1 in Equation 1, showing better results with both $S_1(x,y)$ and $S_2(x,y)$.
The proposed efficient model significantly improves over the baseline, and initial sentences associated with a keyword/topic play a significant role.
